Chapter 4: Addressing Problems Quickly and Fairly
Let’s be honest—no workplace is totally free from mistakes or setbacks. Even when you’ve set clear goals and handed out regular praise, there’ll be times when performance just doesn’t hit the mark. So, what really matters is how leaders respond in those moments. That’s often the difference between sparking real growth... or creating lingering resentment.
Here’s where the third core practice comes in—delivering what’s called a “one-minute reprimand.” It’s all about tackling problems head-on, doing it fast, and always treating people with respect.
Have you ever noticed how some managers avoid giving negative feedback because they worry it’ll hurt morale? Or maybe they wait too long, and those little issues snowball into bigger headaches. The best leaders, though, don’t wait. They deal with concerns as soon as they pop up—honestly, but in a way that’s supportive.
So how does a one-minute reprimand actually work? Here’s the basic process:
First, if a team member’s actions aren’t meeting expectations, the manager addresses it right away. The feedback is clear and specific—focusing on what happened, not attacking the person. Then, the manager explains why this behavior is a problem and how it impacts the team or organization. And finally, after delivering the reprimand, the manager reaffirms their belief in the person’s ability to improve, making sure they know they’re still a valued member of the team.
Imagine someone misses an important deadline. The manager might say, “I noticed the report was submitted late, which delayed the project for everyone. Meeting deadlines is crucial for our success. I know you can do better, and I appreciate your contributions.” See the difference? You’re separating the mistake from the person’s worth. The message is clear: we’re aiming for improvement, not punishment.
This kind of immediate, direct feedback really pays off. It clears up any misunderstandings and lets people fix course quickly. When team members know exactly what went wrong and why it matters, they’re way less likely to repeat the same mistake. Plus, when feedback is fair and focused on actions—not character—it lowers anxiety and defensiveness.
It’s also important to keep reprimands short and to the point. Nobody wants a long lecture or an emotional outburst—that rarely helps anyone. The real goal here is to address the issue, clarify what’s expected, and move forward. When you wrap up with a positive note, you’re showing that you believe in your people and are invested in their growth.
Of course, this practice takes self-awareness. As a leader, you’ve got to be willing to face tough conversations without letting your own frustration or disappointment take over. Remember—everyone slips up sometimes, and feedback should be used as a tool for learning, not as a weapon for blame.
Sometimes, if the same issues keep popping up, it could be a sign of something deeper—maybe unclear goals, not enough training, or even personal struggles. The best managers use reprimands as a way to start a conversation, not just to end one. They listen, ask questions, and work alongside their team members to find real solutions.
When you make one-minute reprimands a regular part of your leadership toolkit, you’re building a culture of accountability and trust. People know that if there’s a problem, it’ll be addressed quickly and fairly—not left to fester. That kind of clarity helps everyone focus on getting better, instead of dwelling on mistakes.
And when you combine this with clear goals and immediate praise, you create a balanced, supportive environment where everyone can do their best work. Mistakes become chances to grow, and feedback turns into a shared language for success.
